title: How Much to Bet
author: William Poundstone
wiifm: You can be right about a good opportunity and still be destroyed by it, simply by staking too much. This is the story of two men: a chain-smoking Texan physicist at Bell Labs who found the mathematical answer to how much you should bet and died at forty-one without knowing it would bear his name, and the young mathematician who took that answer to the blackjack tables of Nevada and then to Wall Street. It ends with two Nobel laureates who ignored it. You will come away knowing how to size every commitment in your business.

b: John Larry Kelly Junior was born on Boxing Day 1923 in Corsicana, a small oil town in east Texas. He grew up with a drawl he never lost, a quick mind for numbers and, later, a serious cigarette habit. In the Second World War he served four years as a pilot in the United States Navy.

After the war he went to the University of Texas at Austin and took a doctorate in physics in 1953. Then he joined Bell Labs in New Jersey, the research arm of the American telephone monopoly AT&T, and at that moment probably the most creative scientific workplace on earth. The transistor had been invented there a few years before.

Kelly was the kind of colleague people remembered. He liked guns and American football, and he liked betting on the football. He was also a gifted, wide-ranging scientist who worked on television signals and, in 1961, helped make a computer sing. With colleagues including the music pioneer Max Mathews, he programmed an IBM computer to sing the old song Daisy Bell, one of the first convincing demonstrations of computer speech. The story goes that the writer Arthur C. Clarke heard it on a visit to Bell Labs, and it became the song the dying computer HAL sings in 2001: A Space Odyssey.
But the thing that matters for this book was a nine-page paper he wrote in 1956, which more or less solved the oldest practical question in risk.
ch.cap: Kelly's IBM sings Daisy Bell at Bell Labs, 1961

b: A few doors from Kelly worked Claude Shannon, the shy genius who in 1948 had published A Mathematical Theory of Communication and in doing so invented information theory. Shannon showed that information could be measured in bits, and that any communication channel, a telephone line, a radio link, has a maximum rate at which it can carry information reliably, however noisy it is. He called that its capacity.

Shannon was also a famous tinkerer, who rode a unicycle along the Bell Labs corridors and built juggling machines and a mechanical mouse that could learn a maze. He was fascinated by games, and by whether mathematics could beat them.
Kelly took Shannon's ideas somewhere Shannon had not. And he got there by thinking about crime.

This is the question that runs through the whole week, and Kelly was about to answer it. Suppose, after everything Taleb, Meadows, Perrow and Tetlock have said, you do have a real edge in an uncertain situation. There is still a number you must choose every single time, and it decides your fate more than the quality of your insight. How much do you bet?
ch.cap: Shannon unicycles and juggles past Kelly at Bell Labs

ch.h: The man with the private wire
b: In the nineteen-fifties American horse-racing results reached bookmakers by telegraph and telephone wire, and the racing wire was big business. Poundstone notes that a wire service run in its day by the publisher Moses Annenberg was among AT&T's largest customers. There was a known scam called past-posting: if you could learn a result before the bookmaker did, you could bet on a race that had already been run.

Kelly imagined something subtler. Suppose a gambler has a friend at the track telephoning tips down a noisy line, so some of what he hears is right and some is garbled. And Kelly saw that a gambler receiving imperfect information is mathematically the same thing as Shannon's noisy channel. The result is one of the loveliest in applied mathematics. The fastest rate at which the gambler's wealth can grow is exactly equal to the information capacity of his private wire. Your edge turns into compound growth at a fixed rate. Betting harder cannot buy you a faster one. It can only buy you a slower one.

He wanted to call the paper Information Theory and Gambling. AT&T's executives, running a regulated monopoly and keen not to be linked to bookmakers, objected. It appeared in the Bell System Technical Journal in 1956 under the bland title A New Interpretation of Information Rate, which is one reason economists ignored it for years.

Kelly never cashed in. On 18 March 1965 he collapsed on a Manhattan pavement from a brain haemorrhage and died, aged forty-one. He almost certainly had no idea that his paper would become the Kelly criterion.
ch.cap: A garbled tip runs down the wire from the track

b: In its simplest form the rule is almost insultingly short. Bet a fixed fraction of your current wealth, and make that fraction your edge divided by the odds. For an even-money bet that is simply your chance of winning minus your chance of losing. If you have a fifty-five per cent chance at even money, bet ten per cent of your pot. Not a penny more, however confident you feel.

What the rule really does is maximise the long-run growth rate of your wealth, which is the average of what happens to one person over time, not the average across many people at once. That difference is the most valuable idea in the book, and a coin shows it.

Imagine a coin where heads wins eighty per cent of your stake and tails loses fifty per cent. The average outcome is superb, plus fifteen per cent a flip, so any simple expected-value sum says bet everything every time. Do that, and one head and one tail multiply your wealth by one point eight and then by a half, leaving you with nine-tenths of where you started. Over a hundred flips, you are left with about half of one per cent of your money. A wonderful bet, taken at full size, is a reliable road to ruin.

Now bet Kelly's fraction, which for this coin is three-eighths of your wealth each flip. The same coin now grows your money by nearly three per cent a flip. Nothing about the bet changed. Only the size. Because a fifty per cent loss needs a hundred per cent gain to recover, gains and losses do not cancel. And because you always bet a fraction of what remains, you can never reach zero. The idea had an ancestor: in 1738 Daniel Bernoulli proposed the same logarithmic thinking to solve a famous puzzle about a wager with infinite expected value. Kelly rediscovered it from a different direction, which usually means something real is there.
ch.cap: Same coin: all-in shrinks the pile, Kelly's fraction grows it

ch.h: The boy who blew things up
b: The man who turned Kelly's paper into money was Edward Thorp. Born in Chicago in 1932 and raised in southern California through the Depression and the war, he was a self-taught prodigy who as a teenager ran his own chemistry experiments, including, by his own cheerful account, a fair few explosions. He took a doctorate in mathematics at UCLA and by 1959 was teaching at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

On a holiday in Las Vegas he became convinced that blackjack could be beaten. Unlike roulette, the cards are dealt without being put back, so as the deck is used up the odds shift, and sometimes they shift in the player's favour. Using an IBM computer he worked out exactly when. What he lacked was a rule for how much to bet when the odds turned his way, and a colleague pointed him to Kelly's paper. In January 1961 he presented his system to the American Mathematical Society under the title Fortune's Formula: The Game of Blackjack. Poundstone took his book's title from that talk.

Then he tested it. According to Thorp's own account, two wealthy gamblers with underworld connections, Manny Kimmel and Eddie Hand, put up ten thousand dollars, and over a weekend in Reno and Lake Tahoe Thorp roughly doubled it, betting small when the deck was against him and more when it was rich, always as a fraction of his bankroll.
He published Beat the Dealer in 1962. It became a bestseller, and the casinos responded by changing their rules, adding more decks, and barring card counters.
ch.cap: Thorp counts cards in Reno while his backers watch

b: Before the book came out, Thorp had gone to see Claude Shannon about the blackjack paper, and the two found they shared an obsession with beating games. They spent months in the basement workshop of Shannon's rambling house in Winchester, outside Boston, building a machine to beat roulette.

It is now generally regarded as the first wearable computer. One person timed the ball and the spinning wheel with switches worked by the toes inside a shoe. The device then sent a musical tone through a wire to an earpiece, telling the bettor which eighth of the wheel the ball was likely to land in.

In the summer of 1961 they took it to Las Vegas, with their wives as lookouts. The predictions worked. What defeated them was a wire. The fine lead to the earpiece kept breaking, and on one occasion a woman at the next table stared in alarm at the thing poking from Thorp's ear. They packed up and went home.
The failure is worth remembering. The mathematics was never the weak point. It was a wire and a stranger's curiosity. Clever systems are usually brought down by something with no place in the model.
ch.cap: A wire pokes from Thorp's ear; a stranger stares

b: Thorp then turned to a bigger casino. With Sheen Kassouf he wrote Beat the Market in 1967, about pricing warrants and options, and he worked out a method for valuing options before the famous Black and Scholes formula was published. In 1969 he co-founded a fund that became Princeton Newport Partners, arguably the first quantitative hedge fund.

Over about nineteen years it returned roughly fifteen per cent a year after fees, without a single losing year. That last fact is the secret. Thorp used Kelly not as a target to bet the maximum, but as a ceiling. He knew his estimate of his edge could be wrong, so he usually bet less than the formula said.

The fund was not killed by markets. In December 1987 federal agents raided its Princeton office as part of an investigation run from Rudolph Giuliani's office in New York, using racketeering laws designed for organised crime. Several Princeton partners were convicted on charges connected to tax trades, and most of those convictions were later overturned on appeal. Thorp, based in California, was never charged. But the fund did not survive the process.
Poundstone's point is sharp. The model was right about the markets. It had no term for the Department of Justice. That is Taleb's casino tiger again, the risk outside the spreadsheet.
ch.cap: Federal agents carry files out of Princeton Newport, 1987

b: You might expect economists to have welcomed such a powerful formula. Many did the opposite, and the fight is the liveliest strand in the book.

On one side stood the Kelly camp, Kelly, Thorp, the economist Henry Latane and the statistician Leo Breiman, arguing that it was the best possible strategy: it maximised growth, never risked ruin, and in the long run beat any other system with near certainty. On the other side stood Paul Samuelson of MIT, perhaps the most powerful economist of the century, who thought calling it optimal was a mistake.

His argument was technically correct. Kelly is only best if your attitude to risk happens to be logarithmic, and that is an assumption about your tastes, not a law of mathematics. Someone who values certainty more than growth should rationally bet less. Samuelson pressed the point for years with open scorn, and in 1979 published a paper written almost entirely in words of one syllable, so that nobody could claim the argument was too subtle.

Both sides won something. Samuelson was right that Kelly is not optimal for everyone. But the Kelly camp was right about the part that matters most. Betting more than Kelly is bad for anyone, whatever their tastes, because it lowers your growth and raises your risk at the same time. The curve is lopsided. Half Kelly gives you roughly three-quarters of the growth with about half the swings. Twice Kelly gives you a long-run growth rate of about zero. Beyond that you go broke, even with a genuine edge. And since you never know your edge exactly, estimation error is always a reason to bet less, never more.
ch.cap: The lopsided curve: at twice Kelly, growth falls to zero

b: The book ends with the perfect cautionary tale. Long-Term Capital Management began trading in February 1994, founded by the bond trader John Meriwether. Its partners included Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who shared the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1997 for their work on pricing options. These were among the cleverest financial minds who have ever lived. After fees the fund made about twenty-one per cent in its first part-year, then forty-three, then forty-one.

Its trades were bets on tiny mispricings between closely related bonds, so the edge on each was small, and the only way to make big returns was borrowing. At the start of 1998 the fund had about four point seven billion dollars of its own money supporting around a hundred and twenty-nine billion dollars of assets, borrowing more than twenty-five dollars for every one of its own.

Then in August 1998 Russia defaulted on its debts. Positions the models treated as unrelated all moved the same way at once, as things do in a panic. The fund lost about four point six billion dollars in under four months. On 23 September 1998 the Federal Reserve Bank of New York gathered fourteen banks, which put in about three point six billion dollars to take it over and wind it down in an orderly way, for fear that a disorderly collapse would damage the whole system.

Here is the sting. Many of their bets were broadly right, and the gaps they had bet on largely closed in time, without them. They had a real edge and lost almost everything, because of the one decision that is not an insight at all: how much.
ch.cap: LTCM's borrowed tower teeters as Russia defaults, 1998

ch.h: Still there for the next bet
b: Long-Term Capital gathers the whole week in one story. Its models used mild-world tools in a wild world, as Taleb warned. Hidden links between positions only showed up under stress, as Meadows would have predicted. The system was complex and tightly coupled, with no time to think, as Perrow described. Its confidence had never been tested against a record long enough to include a crisis, as Tetlock would insist. And its sizing was wrong, which on its own would have been enough to save it.

Kelly has limits, and Poundstone is honest about them. It needs a known edge, and in business you only ever have an estimate, coloured by enthusiasm. Full Kelly is wild, with drops of half your wealth to be expected, and a strategy you abandon at the bottom is worse than a smaller one you keep. And the maths assumes endless repeated bets with no deadlines, while real life has a tax bill in January and a payroll at month end.

So use Kelly as Thorp did, as a ceiling. Size each commitment as a share of what you could lose and still keep trading. Before any personal guarantee, uncapped contract, remortgage or big hire, ask: if this goes to zero on Monday, can I still make the next move? Look at your biggest client too. If one client is forty per cent of your turnover, you are holding a large position on someone else's goodwill, and the fix is to win other work while things are good.

John Kelly died on a New York pavement without knowing what he had found. Ed Thorp, now in his nineties, lived to see it proved. The quality of your bets decides whether you make money. The size of them decides whether you are still there to make the next one.
ch.cap: Thorp bets a slice, keeping enough for the next hand

take: Your edge has a speed limit
Kelly proved that an edge turns into growth at a fixed maximum rate. Betting harder cannot speed it up and will slow it down.
Staking a share of what you have means you can never hit zero. For an even-money bet, the share is your chance of winning minus your chance of losing.
Distrust the average in repeated games
The plus eighty, minus fifty coin averages plus fifteen per cent yet ruins you at full stake. Judge repeated decisions by what happens to you over time.
Half Kelly keeps most of the growth with half the swings, while twice Kelly earns nothing. Over-betting costs everything, under-betting only a little.
You only ever estimate your edge, and enthusiasm inflates it. Uncertainty about the odds is always a reason to bet less.
Work out what share of revenue and profit your largest client is. Above about a quarter, win other work while things are good.
Before any guarantee, uncapped liability or big commitment, ask whether you could still make the next move if it went to zero.
Brilliance is no margin of safety
LTCM had Nobel laureates and a real edge, and lost almost everything through leverage. Clever ideas never excuse oversized bets.
recall: What did Kelly prove about information and wealth?

That the fastest possible growth rate of a gambler's wealth equals the information capacity of the channel carrying his edge, Shannon's measure. Betting more aggressively cannot raise that rate and over-betting lowers it.
Why does the plus eighty, minus fifty coin ruin you at full stake?

A win and a loss multiply your wealth by one point eight and then a half, leaving nine-tenths, so you shrink about five per cent a flip and keep about half a per cent after a hundred flips. Betting three-eighths of your wealth instead turns the same coin into growth of nearly three per cent a flip.
How did Thorp use Kelly, and with what result?

He used it to size blackjack bets and then trades, treating it as a ceiling and usually betting less. Princeton Newport made roughly fifteen per cent a year after fees for about nineteen years without a losing year.
What was Samuelson's objection, and what survived it?

He argued Kelly is only optimal if your attitude to risk is logarithmic, so calling it best smuggles in a value judgement. What survived is that betting above Kelly lowers growth and raises risk for anyone.
Why did Long-Term Capital Management fail?

It made small-edge trades with leverage above twenty-five to one, and when Russia defaulted in 1998 supposedly unrelated positions moved together. It lost about four point six billion dollars in under four months despite having a genuine edge.
note: Kelly's paper appeared in the Bell System Technical Journal in July 1956; the original title and AT&T's objection are as Poundstone reports. Accounts differ on which IBM machine and which colleagues produced the 1961 Daisy Bell demonstration, and the Clarke link rests on later recollection. The Reno and Tahoe test with Kimmel and Hand rests on Thorp's own account. Princeton Newport's returns are commonly cited figures; most convictions of its partners were overturned on appeal and Thorp was never charged. LTCM figures follow the President's Working Group report of 1999 and Roger Lowenstein's When Genius Failed.
words: Describing a process where the average across many people at once equals the average one person experiences over time.
Poundstone's coin is non-ergodic: it averages plus fifteen per cent a flip across a crowd, yet one person betting everything on every flip is almost certainly ruined.
Growing or measured by multiplication rather than addition, so equal percentage changes count equally.
The Kelly criterion maximises the logarithm of wealth, the same logic Daniel Bernoulli proposed in 1738, which is why it treats a fifty per cent loss as needing a hundred per cent gain to undo.
Profiting from a price gap between two closely related assets that should be worth the same.
Long-Term Capital Management's trades were arbitrage on tiny bond mispricings, so small that only enormous borrowing could make them pay.
Running an ongoing illegal enterprise, and in American law the basis for sweeping charges designed for organised crime.
Princeton Newport Partners was brought down when federal prosecutors used racketeering laws against its Princeton office in 1987, though most convictions were later overturned.
The spread of a shock from one market or institution to others, like an infection.
When Russia defaulted in August 1998, contagion made positions that LTCM's models treated as unrelated all move against it together.
stories: In 1956 John Kelly, a chain-smoking Texan physicist at Bell Labs, imagined a gambler with a friend at the racetrack phoning tips down a noisy line. Kelly saw that this was exactly Claude Shannon's noisy channel, and proved that the fastest the gambler's wealth could grow equalled the capacity of his private wire. Betting harder could not speed it up, only slow it down. He wanted to call it Information Theory and Gambling. AT&T, a regulated monopoly keen not to be linked with bookmakers, objected, and it appeared as A New Interpretation of Information Rate. In 1965 Kelly collapsed on a Manhattan pavement and died at forty-one, never knowing the rule would bear his name.

In 1960 the young mathematician Edward Thorp, fresh from cracking blackjack, went to see Claude Shannon, the father of information theory. They spent months in the basement of Shannon's house outside Boston building a machine to beat roulette, now generally regarded as the first wearable computer. One person timed the ball and wheel with toe switches inside a shoe; a musical tone in an earpiece told the bettor which eighth of the wheel to back. In the summer of 1961 they tried it in Las Vegas, wives as lookouts. The predictions worked. The fragile earpiece wire kept breaking, and a woman at the next table stared at the thing poking from Thorp's ear. They went home.
Two Nobel laureates and a default

Long-Term Capital Management started trading in 1994 with partners including Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who shared the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1997. Their bets on tiny gaps between related bonds were clever, but the edge was so small that big returns needed huge borrowing: by early 1998, about four point seven billion dollars of its own capital supported around a hundred and twenty-nine billion of assets. In August Russia defaulted, everything moved together, and the fund lost about four point six billion in under four months. The New York Fed gathered fourteen banks to take it over. The sting: many trades came right later, without them.
biz: Before any big commitment, such as a twelve-month software contract, a new hire, a large ad test or a personal guarantee, write down the worst case and compare it with what the business could lose and still trade normally. Treat your estimate of the upside as inflated, as Thorp did, and size at roughly half what feels justified. For ad tests, cap each one at a small, fixed share of the monthly budget, increase only after cost per completed case is proven over a full lending cycle, and cut back quickly when it is not. Measure months of operating cash held, and never let a single bet threaten it.

If one lender takes most of your completions, or one ad platform supplies most of your enquiries, you are holding an oversized position on someone else's decisions. Check the figures this week: share of completions by lender, and share of enquiries by Google, Bing, Facebook and organic search. Where any single source is over about forty per cent, start broadening while things are good, by strengthening SEO and testing other channels. On lenders, diversify only by adding products that genuinely suit customers' needs; Consumer Duty means a customer's recommendation must never be steered by which lender pays you more.
connects: Housel's insistence on room for error and staying in the game is Kelly's lesson in plain words: avoid ruin first, because compounding only works for those who survive.
Munger's advice to bet heavily only when the odds are strongly in your favour, and otherwise to wait, is a practical cousin of sizing bets by the size of your edge.
Taleb's warning about ruin in Extremistan and Kelly's proof that over-betting destroys even a genuine edge meet in the collapse of Long-Term Capital Management.
recap:
John Kelly was born in Corsicana, Texas, on Boxing Day nineteen twenty-three. He flew for the American Navy in the war, took a doctorate in physics, and joined Bell Labs, where a few doors away sat Claude Shannon, the inventor of information theory. In nineteen fifty-six Kelly wrote a nine-page paper about a gambler with a noisy private wire from the racetrack, and proved something lovely. The fastest your wealth can grow from an edge is fixed by the quality of your information. Betting harder cannot make it faster. It can only make it slower. The company made him give the paper a dull title, and in nineteen sixty-five he died on a Manhattan pavement, aged forty-one, never knowing the rule would carry his name.

The rule is simple. Bet a fixed fraction of what you have, set by the size of your edge. With a fifty-five per cent chance at even money, bet ten per cent. The deeper lesson is that the average across many people is not what happens to one person over time. A coin that pays eighty per cent on heads and loses fifty on tails looks wonderful on average, yet staking everything on every flip leaves you with almost nothing. Bet the right fraction and the same coin makes you richer.

The man who proved it in the real world was Edward Thorp, a young mathematician who worked out how to beat blackjack, used Kelly to size his bets, and by his own account doubled a ten thousand dollar stake over a weekend in Nevada. With Shannon he built a computer hidden in a shoe to beat roulette. The maths worked. A fragile earpiece wire did not. Thorp then ran a hedge fund for about nineteen years without a losing year, because he treated Kelly as a ceiling, not a target. The fund was ended not by markets but by a federal raid, and Thorp was never charged.

Economists led by Paul Samuelson argued that Kelly was not best for everyone, and they had a point. But betting more than Kelly is bad for anyone, and since you never know your edge exactly, error is always a reason to bet less.

Then came Long-Term Capital Management, with two Nobel laureates among its partners and more than twenty-five borrowed dollars for every one of its own. In nineteen ninety-eight Russia defaulted, its bets all moved together, and it lost about four point six billion dollars in under four months. Many of its trades were right. Its sizing was not.

The line to remember: the quality of your bets decides whether you make money, and their size decides whether you survive to bet again.
